summary.verdict: Your page has something most winners lack: pre- and post-surveys at every school level, and tables that pair each piece of feedback with the change you made. What holds it back is order and accuracy. Your reason for teaching sits in section 4, each school level is told twice (sections 4 and 5), and about twenty numbers, labels and captions disagree with each other.
strengths: Pre- and post-surveys at all three levels, with results per question. Among the six winners, only Heidelberg measured learning.
Elementary feedback tables that pair each issue, in the students' or teacher's words, with the change you made, trial by trial.
Honest reporting of weak spots: the Q1 dip, the 30% base-pairing score, and the high school line “we did not sufficiently consider”.
Reusable detail: debate timings, game rules, and lesson plans and bilingual slides as downloads.
Experiments that link to ReLeaf through science (heat on leaf disks, salt on onion cells), with no selling.
priorities: Rewrite the abstract sheet, the first thing a judge reads. Open with who you taught and how many, and say which school level each number comes from (the 80% is elementary, the 30% is junior high). Bold a result with a number.

Fix the numbers, labels and captions that disagree: trial count, question counts, swapped and mislabelled figures, junior high text copied from the elementary section, and the two card game rule sets. Then read the page aloud once.
Open the page with your purpose, your three audiences and how the 144 students break down. Move the website and the “why” paragraph from section 4.
Turn section 7.2 into proof: three “they said X, so we changed Y” examples you already have, plus what students argued in the debate.
Give the number of students for every survey, say whether the same students answered before and after, and translate the handwritten feedback.
Cut repeats: the leaf-disk experiment (told three times), the website (three times), and sections 7.3 and 7.4.

ballot.question: How well did their work promote mutual learning and/or a dialogue?
ballot.where: 4. Execution: Suggestions & Changes Made tables; 7.2 Mutual Learning and Dialogue
ballot.note: The elementary tables show real feedback loops, but 7.2 only claims dialogue and the debate results are missing.

ballot.question: Is it documented in a way that others can build upon?
ballot.where: 6. Tools/Resources; Lesson Plan downloads in each audience section
ballot.note: Plans, slides and five games are online, but junior high has no lesson plan and the climate card game has two rule sets.

ballot.question: Was it thoughtfully implemented?
ballot.where: 3. Designing The Lesson; 4. Execution (DBTL trials); 5. Impact of Our Lessons
ballot.note: Design steps, trials and changes per trial are strong; junior high and high school lack dates, school names and class sizes up front.

ballot.question: Did the team convince you that their activities would enable more people to shape, contribute to, and/or participate in synthetic biology?
ballot.where: 2.3 Get Involved; 7.5 How we Achieved Sustainable Education
ballot.note: The page says others can use the materials but shows no one who has; add sign-ups, downloads and the teachers who plan to reuse them.

releaf: 4. Execution (elementary, junior high and high school lessons)
5. Impact of Our Lessons (elementary, junior high and high school analysis)
winners: Purpose: why public learning matters, in one or two paragraphs
Structure statement: how the page is organised
Groups of activities, each opening with why this audience
Per activity: setting and headcount, what was taught, the hands-on part, how participants engaged, a measured or quoted outcome, what the team changed, materials to reuse
Forward look: who continues it and where the materials live
skeleton.gap: Your page starts with the website and states its purpose only in section 4. It also splits each school level across sections 4 and 5, so a judge reads each level twice. Put each level's lesson, results and changes under one heading, opened by a short “why this group” paragraph.

extras: “Click Here to Explore Our Website: Gems Taiwan, Home” → “Click Here to Explore Our Website: GEMS Taiwan, Home”. Your team name is written GEMS Taiwan on the Entrepreneurship page. Fix both copies of this link line.

“engineered PGPR bioreactors for crop protection” → “an engineered B. subtilis bioreactor for crop protection”. The Human Practices page says you moved away from a broad PGPR system to a controlled bioreactor.

“having a full run-through session of our lesson, and lastly communicating and reaching out to schools” → “communicating and reaching out to schools, and lastly having a full run-through session”. The folds below put contacting schools third and run-throughs fourth. Make the list match.
“whether the content we were planning on teaching were already being taught” → “whether the content we were planning to teach was already being taught”. “Content” is singular.
“each of our sessions are structured” → “each of our sessions is structured”. “Each” takes a singular verb.
“engage students into learning” → “engage students in learning”. The verb “engage” goes with “in”.
“Trial 1 (June 25th/26th, 2026)” → “Trial 1 (June 25th–26th, 2026)”. Trial 1 is written three ways (“June 25th/26th”, “June 25th-26th”, “6/25+26”). Pick one date style for the whole page.
“Spend more time on explaining vocabulary and broke down” → “Spent more time explaining vocabulary and broke down”. The other rows in this column are in the past tense.

“we plan to have a strict 1:5 mentor-to-student ratio” → “we used a 1:5 mentor-to-student ratio from Trial [number]”. A plan sits in the “Changes Made” column. Say whether you made the change, and when.

“Our team visited 1 junior high school” → “Our team visited one junior high school”. Write numbers under ten as words in sentences. The same goes for “visited 3 elementary schools” and “visited 1 high school”.

“an online game that allows student to apply different amount of vital necessities” → “an online game that lets students change the amount of each thing plants need”. “Students” and “amounts” need to be plural.
“based off the topic” → “based on the topic”. “Based on” is the standard phrase.
“answered the DNA base-pairing question correct after the lesson” → “answered the DNA base-pairing question correctly after the lesson”. “Answered” needs the adverb “correctly”.
“After concluding the experiment section, we briefly reviewed” → “After this section, we briefly reviewed”. The section just before this one is Synthetic Biology, not the experiment.
“how genetic information is translated and transcribed” → “how genetic information is transcribed and translated”. Transcription happens first, so name it first.

“This page presents a comprehensive analysis of all the data” → “This section shows the data”. It is a section of the Education page, not a page. The high school analysis also starts with “This page presents”.

“A. Emotion & Attitude (A–D), Agree/Neutral/Disagree” → “Agree/Neutral/Disagree, with charts that report % Agree”. The survey scale is Agree/Neutral/Disagree, but Fig. 3 and the text count % “Yes”. Use one scale name.

“A. Emotional & Attitude (A–F), Yes/Somewhat/No” → “A. Emotion & Attitude (A–F), Yes/Somewhat/No”. The elementary and high school lists say “Emotion & Attitude”. Use the same label for all three levels.

“P. Future Action (G–J), Agree/Neutral/Disagree” → “P. Future Action (F–I), Agree/Neutral/Disagree”. The high school letters jump from E to G. Either add F or relabel G to J as F to I, and match the charts.

“Since primary school students possess varying levels” → “Since elementary school students have varying levels”. The page says “elementary” and “junior high” everywhere else, but also uses “primary, middle, or high school” in Design Process. Pick one set of names.

“They were underscoring how effective physical, interactive game mechanics were at driving engagement.” → “This shows how well physical, hands-on games kept students engaged.”. The students were not “underscoring” anything. This sentence is your conclusion, so say it in your own voice.
“pointing lecture style teaching segments as the weak link” → “pointing to lecture-style teaching as the weak part”. “Pointing” needs “to”.
“which increased by 49%” → “which rose by 49 percentage points (from [x]% to [y]%)”. “Increased by 49%” can mean two different things. Give the before and after scores.
“the workshop's games, hands-on elements were its strongest asset” → “the workshop’s games and hands-on activities were its strongest part”. An “and” is missing between the two items.

“more than 22 out of 28 students answered each question correctly” → “at least 22 of 28 students answered each question correctly”. The chart shows some questions at exactly 22, so “more than 22” is wrong.

On this page map: “Preparation · Mission & Vision”, “Designing The Lesson · Design Process” and the other rows repeat subheading names. Fix: one line that says what each section shows, for example “Execution · The three lessons, one per school level”.
“Three Trials at a Glance” (the section 4 table heading and the map line for Execution) → “Four Trials at a Glance”. The table lists four: Preliminary, Trial 1, Trial 2 and Trial 3.
On this page map: “6–7 · Resources and impacts · Educational Tools & Resources” → two rows, “6 · Tools/Resources” and “7 · Long Term Impacts”. Section 7 has no line of its own on the map.
“Designing The Lesson” → “Designing the Lesson”. The heading and the map use a capital “The”; the other headings use normal title case.

notes.anchor: Our education program focuses on helping students understand plant stress, climate change, sustainability, and synthetic biology
notes.title: Lead with who you taught
notes.body: This is the first sentence a judge reads, and it only names topics. It is copied from section 7.1. Say who you taught, how many and how.
notes.after: We taught 144 students at five schools in Taiwan, from grade 4 to grade 12, about plant stress, climate change and synthetic biology through hands-on lessons.
notes.excerpt_note: Aachen gives the gap and its answer in five sentences. Heidelberg names every activity in its opening paragraph.

notes.anchor: and learned from survey results and feedback
notes.title: Name one thing you changed
notes.body: The first ballot question is about mutual learning, and this is the only line on the sheet that touches it. Say one thing you changed because of feedback.
notes.after: and changed the lesson after each visit. When students said “too much english”, we broke vocabulary into simpler words.
notes.excerpt_note: Whose feedback, then what changed, in two sentences.
notes.ballot: How well did their work promote mutual learning and/or a dialogue?

notes.anchor: Our program and lesson plan meaningfully improved students’ understanding of synthetic biology and plant science concepts
notes.title: Put a number in bold
notes.body: This sentence comes from the elementary summary, but here it speaks for all three levels. “Meaningfully improved” is the bold message, and it has no number. Bold a result a judge can check.
notes.after: Correct answers rose from [x]% before the lesson to [y]% after, across [number] students.

notes.anchor: DNA base pairing remained a challenging concept
notes.title: A weak result on the first screen
notes.body: You put a result that did not go well in bold, right at the top. Judges trust a team that shows its weak spots, and it makes your other claims easier to believe.
notes.excerpt_note: Heidelberg says plainly that an event missed its audience, then what the team took from it.

notes.anchor: with only 30% of students answering correctly after the lesson
notes.title: The 30% is junior high only
notes.body: Here it reads as if only 30% of all 144 students got DNA base pairing right. In the body, 30% is the junior high result, and the elementary analysis says the DNA question went from “at or below 25% accuracy and jumping to around 90%”. Say which level.
notes.after: Junior high students found it hardest: only 30% answered correctly after the lesson.

notes.anchor: All three teachers who took the survey indicated they would be willing to continue participating.
notes.title: A real count of teachers
notes.body: “All three teachers” is a number a judge can check, and it shows others plan to carry on your work. Add that they were elementary teachers, and mention the high school teacher who plans to use your slides.
notes.ballot: Did the team convince you that their activities would enable more people to shape, contribute to, and/or participate in synthetic biology?

notes.anchor: a centralized center where students and educators
notes.title: This line stops mid-sentence
notes.body: The line is cut from a longer sentence, so it ends on “students and educators” with no verb. “Centralized center” also says the same thing twice. Say what the website gives people.
notes.after: free lesson plans, slides and games for teachers and students

notes.anchor: 144 students; 5 schools
notes.title: Show what the 144 is made of
notes.body: This row is reach, so it is labelled “Impact of Our Lessons” by mistake. The body never shows how 144 adds up: the tables give 99 elementary and 28 high school students, and no junior high count. Add the split you already know.
notes.after: 144 students; 5 schools (3 elementary, 1 junior high, 1 high school)

notes.anchor: all questions scoring at least an 80% in accuracy
notes.title: This is the elementary result only
notes.body: The row says every question reached 80%, but the next row says “only 30% of students answering correctly”. The 80% is from the elementary analysis. The high school chart shows some questions at 22 of 28 (79%). Say which level.
notes.after: Elementary: every question at least 80% correct after the lesson

notes.anchor: freely accessible to educators, students
notes.title: Say what can be reused
notes.body: The line ends after “students,” because it was cut short. A judge wants to know what they could take away. Count your downloads and games.
notes.after: 2 lesson plans, 3 slide decks, 2 card games, 2 online games and a plant stress simulator, free online
notes.excerpt_note: Queens lists exactly which materials were handed over and where they live.
notes.ballot: Is it documented in a way that others can build upon?

notes.anchor: To make synthetic biology and the iGEM competition accessible, engaging, and inclusive for everyone, we created a dedicated education website.
notes.title: Open with who you taught and why
notes.body: Your page starts with the website, so a judge meets a tool before learning who you taught and why. Winning pages open with the purpose, the audiences and one number. Start with your lessons and move the website later.
notes.after: We taught 144 students at five schools in [city], from grade 4 to grade 12. Each lesson linked plant stress and climate change to synthetic biology. This page shows how we planned the lessons, what students learned, what we changed after each visit, and the materials you can reuse.
notes.excerpt_note: Queens gives purpose and audience in one paragraph. Heidelberg names every activity in its first lines.

notes.anchor: Through our promotion, we introduce topics like synthetic biology in a simple and engaging way
notes.title: “Promotion” sounds like marketing
notes.body: The prize text asks for scientific learning and rules out marketing synthetic biology or iGEM. The word “promotion” works against you. Your Entrepreneurship page makes it worse: it calls educational outreach “Another one of our sales strategies”. Use “lessons” here, and ask the Entrepreneurship writers to reword their line.
notes.after: In our lessons, we introduce synthetic biology in a simple way, even to students with no biology background.

notes.anchor: could serve as a centralized center where students and educators alike could easily be able to freely access things
notes.title: Say it in fewer words
notes.body: “Centralized center” says the same thing twice, and “could easily be able to freely” stacks three soft words. Short sentences are easier for judges to read.
notes.after: So we built a website where students and teachers can download our lesson plans, slides and games for free.

notes.anchor: Invites teachers, students, and community members to connect with our team directly.
notes.title: Show who used the sign-up form
notes.body: This form is your best answer to the last ballot question: can more people take part? Right now the page only says the form exists. Add how many teachers or schools used it, even if the number is small.
notes.after: Teachers and students can contact us here. By [date], [number] teachers had used this form to ask for a workshop or materials.
notes.ballot: Did the team convince you that their activities would enable more people to shape, contribute to, and/or participate in synthetic biology?

notes.anchor: we also took the time to verify whether the content we were planning on teaching were already being taught in schools
notes.title: You checked the school curriculum first
notes.body: You checked what schools already teach, so your lessons add something new. Judges read this as careful design. Add one line naming the curriculum or grades you checked.
notes.excerpt_note: CityU names what the school curriculum leaves out before saying what they did.
notes.ballot: Was it thoughtfully implemented?

notes.anchor: In the world we live in nowadays, synthetic biology and other related areas are often associated with negative perceptions
notes.title: Move your reason to the top
notes.body: This paragraph is your reason for teaching, but it sits in section 4, after the website and the lesson design. Move it to the top of the page. Cut the sentence about debates that “erupted”: it has no source, and judges already know about the debate.
notes.after: Many students in Taiwan have few chances to learn about synthetic biology, climate change and sustainability through hands-on lessons. Synthetic biology also faces public doubt about safety and ethics. We wanted students of every age to learn the science and discuss it with facts.
notes.excerpt_note: Aachen states the gap and its response in five short sentences, before any detail.

notes.anchor: where we designed the lessons and materials, built and prepared the educational activities, tested them through implementation in schools
notes.title: You used the DBTL cycle for teaching
notes.body: You took the engineering cycle (Design, Build, Test, Learn) and used it on your lessons. Then you show the changes trial by trial. That is strong proof of careful planning, and Aachen won with the same move.
notes.excerpt_note: Aachen shows each format, the feedback on it, and the next version.
notes.ballot: Was it thoughtfully implemented?

notes.anchor: Lastly, to ensure long-term impact, we promoted sustainable education through our website
notes.title: This paragraph repeats section 2
notes.body: Section 2 already explains the website, and section 7 explains long-term impact. This paragraph says it a third time. Replace it with one line.
notes.after: All our materials are free on our education website (see section 6).

notes.anchor: These lessons were made for elementary students ranging from fourth to sixth grade
notes.title: Give ages for international judges
notes.body: Judges from other countries may not know Taiwan’s grade levels. Add the ages once. Also write “synthetic biology” in full before you use “Synbio”.
notes.after: These lessons were for students in grades 4 to 6 (ages [9 to 12]).

notes.anchor: we separated the five lessons we held into three different trials
notes.title: Three trials or four?
notes.body: This sentence says “three different trials” and then lists four: Preliminary, Trial 1, Trial 2 and Trial 3. Your analysis later says “Across our four trials”. Pick one count and use it everywhere.
notes.after: We split the five lessons into four trials: Preliminary (June 24th, 2026), Trial 1 (June 25th and 26th), Trial 2 (June 29th) and Trial 3 (July 14th).

notes.anchor: To connect back to the core idea of our project, we introduced heat as a variable in the experiment
notes.title: Heat links the lesson to ReLeaf
notes.body: The leaf-disk experiment is a classic, but you added heat, the stress your project works on. Students saw the problem with their own eyes. This connects the lesson to your project through science, with no selling.

notes.anchor: Physical Constraints & Ambient Acoustic Audits: Students noted
notes.title: Let the student quotes speak
notes.body: Labels like “Ambient Acoustic Audits” and “Technical Scaffolding for Diverse Fine Motor Skills” are harder to read than the problem itself. The students’ own words already say it. Use short labels.
notes.after: Sound: students said “the sound could be louder”.

notes.anchor: English-language content as barrier
notes.title: Student words, then your change
notes.body: This row has what a judge looks for: the students’ own words, the problem, and what you changed. It answers the mutual learning question directly. Heidelberg wrote the same loop in two sentences.
notes.excerpt_note: Whose feedback, then what changed. Short and easy to check.
notes.ballot: How well did their work promote mutual learning and/or a dialogue?

notes.anchor: Spent more time before the activity to ask and explain to students how this was related to our topic.
notes.title: A teacher’s question changed your lesson
notes.body: A teacher said the planter’s link to the lesson was unclear. You took the comment and changed how you introduced the activity. This is the mutual learning the ballot asks about.
notes.excerpt_note: Aachen credits the person behind a suggestion and names the problem it solved.
notes.ballot: How well did their work promote mutual learning and/or a dialogue?

notes.anchor: Cited issues with discipline at times
notes.title: Put the teacher table in date order
notes.body: The student table goes in date order, but this one jumps from Trial 2 to Trial 1 to Trial 3. Sort it by date, so judges can see each change happen before the next visit.

notes.anchor: In future lessons we could try to teach more in English other than just the vocabulary words
notes.title: Say how you handled mixed feedback
notes.body: Trial 2 students said “too much english”, but the Trial 3 teacher asked for more English. That tension is real dialogue, and judges like to see it. Add one sentence on how you will balance the two.
notes.after: Trial 2 students found the English hard, but the Trial 3 teacher asked for more. Next time we will [plan], so younger students can follow and still practise English.
notes.ballot: How well did their work promote mutual learning and/or a dialogue?

notes.anchor: This interactive workshop successfully bridged complex scientific concepts like synthetic biology and genetics
notes.title: End the section on a result
notes.body: This summary gives a verdict (“successfully bridged”) with no evidence. Your survey numbers are in section 5. Bring one result here, then say what you changed.
notes.after: After four visits, post-survey scores rose on all seven knowledge questions (see section 5). We changed the lesson [number] times based on student and teacher feedback.
notes.excerpt_note: Heidelberg opens each section with three one-line results a judge can skim.

notes.anchor: Our team visited 1 junior high school this year spanning over the months of June and July.
notes.title: Give date, school and class size first
notes.body: A judge checks the date, the school and the number of students first. This sentence has none of them, and one visit cannot span “June and July”. The class size never appears in the junior high sections.
notes.after: On [date], we taught [number] students in grades 7 to 9 at [school name].
notes.ballot: Was it thoughtfully implemented?

notes.anchor: We then moved into a hands-on experiment designed to let students actually watch photosynthesis happen in real time.
notes.title: Do not repeat the experiment text
notes.body: This paragraph repeats the elementary experiment almost word for word, and the high school section tells it a third time. Point back to the first one and say only what was different for this age group.
notes.after: We ran the same spinach leaf-disk experiment as in the elementary lesson (see above). For grades 7 to 9, we [what changed].

notes.anchor: Each round begins by spinning the wheel to reveal a stress.
notes.title: Two different rule sets
notes.body: Here, each round starts with a spin, a combo is a Sensor plus an Action with an optional Boost, and Functional cards steal or swap. In section 6.1 the spin comes after you play, a combo needs “1 Sensor + 1 Action + 1 Boost”, and Gene Coins do the swapping. A teacher cannot run the game if the rules disagree. Keep one version and use it in both places.

notes.anchor: so through this activity students get to understand why exactly synthetic biology is controversial
notes.title: Tell us what the students argued
notes.body: You say the debate shows why synthetic biology is controversial, but you never say what students said. One argument from the Opposing side, and what you learned from it, would be your strongest proof of dialogue.
notes.after: The Opposing team argued that [argument]. We had not thought about [point], and we now [change].
notes.excerpt_note: Heidelberg names one belief the public held and what the team did about it. IISER Pune shows the same claim without an example, and it reads weaker.
notes.ballot: How well did their work promote mutual learning and/or a dialogue?

notes.anchor: Each team selects 3 speakers, who take turns presenting in order, discussing for 45 seconds as a team before each turn
notes.title: A debate any teacher could run
notes.body: You give the team size, the prep time, the speaking times and each speaker’s job. A teacher could run this debate tomorrow. Giving students an Opposing side also shows you teach the science and do not sell it.
notes.excerpt_note: Queens describes a workshop with lengths and station times, so a teacher can plan from it.
notes.ballot: Is it documented in a way that others can build upon?

notes.anchor: Lecture pacing: Some students felt that parts of presentation were too long
notes.title: This table row is broken
notes.body: In the first row, the “Planned Changes” column holds a second issue and no change. So the table never says how you will fix pacing. Move this text to the issue column and write the change.
notes.after: Issue: parts of the lesson were too long (“Spoke for a bit too long”). Planned change: [what you will shorten, and by how much].

notes.anchor: During August, our team visited 1 high school to expand our educational initiative.
notes.title: Add date, school and class size
notes.body: Like the junior high section, this one has no date and no school name, and the class size (28) appears only much later. Put them in the first sentence. “To expand our educational initiative” can go.
notes.after: On [date] in August, we taught 28 students in grades 10 to 12 at [school name].

notes.anchor: we designed a short survey that includes six multiple-choice questions on Kahoot
notes.title: Six questions or seven?
notes.body: Here you say six questions. Your high school survey list in section 5 says “Knowledge (7 benchmark questions)”, and the Fig. 1 chart shows six. Check which is right and fix the other.

notes.anchor: we prepared 3 M and 6 M salt solutions for different groups of students
notes.title: Please check the salt units
notes.body: 6 M salt is close to the most salt water can hold, so a judge may stop here. If you meant percent (for example 3% and 6%), write that. If 3 M and 6 M is right, keep it and name the salt.

notes.anchor: three core categories: Knowledge (K), Attitude (A), and Action (A)
notes.title: Practice or Action?
notes.body: Everywhere else the survey is K-A-P: Knowledge, Attitude, Practice. Here the third part is “Action (A)”. Use one name for the same part at every level.
notes.after: three core categories: Knowledge (K), Attitude (A) and Practice (P).

notes.anchor: At the end of the survey, several students expressed curiosity about how DNA sequences can be modified
notes.title: Do not repeat the table
notes.body: The first two sentences repeat the table above. Start with your own reflection, which is the new part.
notes.after: We taught 28 students in a short time and tried to cover as much as possible. We did not check enough whether they could follow it all. The plasmolysis question had the highest post-survey score, which suggests the hands-on experiment helped.

notes.anchor: we did not sufficiently consider whether the students could effectively absorb and follow all of the information presented
notes.title: You named your own mistake
notes.body: You say you packed in too much and did not check whether students could follow. Admitting a limit like this makes your good results more believable. Queens and Heidelberg both won with sentences like this.
notes.excerpt_note: Both name what went differently from the plan, then what the team took from it.
notes.ballot: How well did their work promote mutual learning and/or a dialogue?

notes.anchor: Together, we organized all the data we received from our surveys into one cohesive analysis
notes.title: Show how 144 adds up
notes.body: This sentence tells the reader nothing new. Use it to break down the 144. Your tables give 99 elementary and 28 high school pre-surveys, and the junior high count is never given, so a judge cannot check the total.
notes.after: We taught 144 students: [99] in elementary school, [number] in junior high and 28 in high school.

notes.anchor: 5.2Specific feedback from students
notes.title: Translate the handwritten feedback
notes.body: Most judges cannot read the Chinese handwriting, so these forms prove nothing to them yet. Add one line of English under each, in the student’s own words.
notes.after: “[English translation of the student’s answer]” (grade [number] student, [school level])
notes.excerpt_note: One student quote with a before and after in it carries more weight than a summary.
notes.ballot: How well did their work promote mutual learning and/or a dialogue?

notes.anchor: The data presented below were obtained through pre- and post-education surveys
notes.title: Give the number of students
notes.body: Every percentage needs its base. Say how many students took each survey, and whether the same students did both. Your pre- and post-survey counts differ (99 and 88), so this matters.
notes.after: [99] students took the pre-survey and [88] took the post-survey. [The same students answered both / Some students answered only one.]
notes.excerpt_note: NYU Abu Dhabi gives the sample size, the count and the percentage together. Heidelberg’s method sentence is clear, but it gives no number of people, so do not copy that gap.
notes.ballot: Was it thoughtfully implemented?

notes.anchor: Fig. 2. Average of Future Attitude & Practice Response
notes.title: Caption does not match the chart
notes.body: Fig. 2 shows knowledge scores before and after the lesson, but its caption says “Future Attitude & Practice Response”. Your own text below says Fig. 1 and Fig. 2 both measure knowledge.
notes.after: Fig. 2. Knowledge results, all four trials combined (pre- vs post-survey, % correct)

notes.anchor: Q1 (Purpose of Photosynthesis) saw a slight dip in Trial 2 before recovering in Trial 3
notes.title: Honest about the weak results
notes.body: You point out where the data is weak: a dip on Q1 and a high starting score on Q2. Judges trust a team that shows its weak spots. Aachen listed its limits before showing its results.
notes.excerpt_note: Aachen says what its version leaves out before comparing results.

notes.anchor: specifically Q4 (Biotic vs. Abiotic Stress) and Q6 (DNA Codons)
notes.title: Base pairing is not a codon
notes.body: Q6 asks how A, T, C and G pair up. A codon is a group of three bases that codes for one amino acid. Your elementary survey list calls this question “DNA and Genetics”, and the junior high list calls it “DNA codons”. Call it “DNA base pairing” everywhere, including the ATCG card game goal.

notes.anchor: toward using plant observation tools, participating in future classes, taking action on plant stress, and engaging with ag-tech
notes.title: These are not the elementary statements
notes.body: The elementary practice statements E to H are about biotechnology, more lessons, problem solving and learning more. The four listed here (plant observation, ag-tech) look like the junior high statements. Check which survey Fig. 4 shows and describe those statements.

notes.anchor: The DNA card game and Kahoot quizzes the most as being the favorites
notes.title: A verb is missing
notes.body: This sentence has no main verb, so it is hard to follow.
notes.after: Students named the DNA card game and the Kahoot quizzes as their favorites most often.

notes.anchor: The consistent gains across all four trials, paired with the direct link between student and teacher feedback
notes.title: “Consistent” clashes with your own data
notes.body: Your Fig. 1 text says Q1 dipped in Trial 2. Here you call the gains “consistent” across all four trials. A judge will notice. Keep the claim as strong as the data.
notes.after: Scores rose after most lessons, and each change we made between visits is listed in the tables above.

notes.anchor: This radar chart plots the percentage of students who agreed with each of six attitude and practice statements
notes.title: Text copied from the elementary section
notes.body: This paragraph describes a radar chart, but the junior high section has none. It uses labels A1 to A3 and P1 to P3, while your survey list uses A to F and G to H, and “knowledge sharing” is not on the list. The Fig. 2 and Fig. 3 captions also say “Across All Four Trials”, but you visited one junior high school. Rewrite this part from the junior high data.

notes.anchor: matching ATCG to itself rather than its complement TAGC
notes.title: One real student error
notes.body: You describe the exact mistake a student made: matching ATCG to ATCG. One concrete error like this proves more than an average. Your planned DNA puzzle kit then closes the loop.
notes.excerpt_note: Heidelberg builds a whole paragraph on one misconception and what the team did next.
notes.ballot: How well did their work promote mutual learning and/or a dialogue?

notes.anchor: understanding of B. subtilis and synthetic biology also increased significantly, from 44% to 80%
notes.title: This question is not in the survey
notes.body: The junior high knowledge list has no question on B. subtilis, so a judge cannot tell where 44% and 80% come from. “Significantly” also suggests a statistics test you do not report. Name the question, or remove the number.
notes.after: Correct answers on [question name] rose from 44% to 80%.

notes.anchor: These findings point to two clear, actionable next steps
notes.title: Two steps promised, one given
notes.body: You promise two next steps but give only one (more hands-on time). Add the second, which is probably the DNA puzzle kit.
notes.after: These findings point to two next steps: more time on hands-on activities, and a color-coded DNA puzzle kit for base pairing.

notes.anchor: the percentage of correct responses to Question 2, which focused on biotic stress, increased from 32% to 96%
notes.title: Numbers with their base
notes.body: You give the class size (28) and the before and after scores for named questions. This is the clearest number reporting on the page. Use it as the model for the elementary and junior high sections.
notes.excerpt_note: NYU Abu Dhabi reports the sample size, the count and the percentage together, just as you do here.
notes.ballot: Was it thoughtfully implemented?

notes.anchor: A majority of students expressed agreement or neutral sentiment toward synthetic biology's real-world value
notes.title: Fig. 2 and Fig. 3 are swapped
notes.body: Real-world value, product awareness and lesson engagement are attitude statements, and they are in Fig. 3. Fig. 2 shows the action statements (notice weather, consider major, share, open to applications). The Fig. 3 caption also says “Action & Sentiment” where it means attitude. Match each paragraph to its chart.

notes.anchor: Despite the experiment, several students also mentioned
notes.title: “Despite” changes the meaning
notes.body: “Despite” means “even though”, so this sentence sounds like the experiment should have stopped students from mentioning the games. You mean “Besides”.
notes.after: Besides the experiment, several students also mentioned

notes.anchor: with a significant majority of the participating students highlighting the card game as the absolute standout
notes.title: Replace big words with your numbers
notes.body: “Absolute standout” and “much more effectively than standard teaching methods” are claims you did not test. You do have data: how many students named the card game as their favorite, and the base-pairing score. Use those.
notes.after: In the elementary post-survey, [number] of [number] students named the card game as their favorite part. Correct answers on base pairing rose from [x]% to [y]%.
notes.excerpt_note: Even winners slip here: CityU gives a postcard swap large claims with no numbers behind them.

notes.anchor: We built this game to make our synthetic biology research fun and easy to understand
notes.title: Give the second card game a name
notes.body: The tab for this game reads “Card Game #2:” with nothing after it, and the text never names the game. The junior high lesson calls it just “a card game”. A name helps teachers find it and talk about it. The tab for Card Game #1 is blank too.

notes.anchor: explains its real mechanism (LEA peptides, NaD1 defensins, Bt toxins)
notes.title: Game protectants differ from your project
notes.body: Cropshield names LEA peptides, NaD1 defensins and Bt toxins. Your Entrepreneurship page names LEA 14, ACCD and NaD1 in one place, and LEA proteins, ACCD and BoPep4 in another. Bt toxins appear on no other ReLeaf page. If the game uses a wider set on purpose, say so; if not, match the project.

notes.anchor: The game includes a bioreactor with a 50% success rate, demonstrating that biological production is not always predictable.
notes.title: The game shows that biology can fail
notes.body: A 50% success rate tells players that production does not always work. That is honest science, and it keeps the game from selling your product. Tying each game rule to a real idea is what makes a game count as teaching.

notes.anchor: designed to fit directly into standard middle and high school STEM curricula
notes.title: Downloads do not match this list
notes.body: This says the lesson plans fit middle and high school. Your downloads are an elementary plan and a high school plan, and junior high has slides only. The list also names biosafety and bioethics, which none of your three lessons describe. Make the list match the files.
notes.ballot: Is it documented in a way that others can build upon?

notes.anchor: Our Education was implemented in a way where both sides were mutually able to contribute to the conversation
notes.title: Prove mutual learning with your examples
notes.body: This section answers the first ballot question, but only with claims. You already have the proof elsewhere on the page. Bring two or three examples here, each written as “they said X, so we changed Y”.
notes.after: Students and teachers changed our lessons. Trial 2 students said “too much english”, so we broke vocabulary into simpler words. A teacher asked how the planter linked to the topic, so we explained it before the activity. A junior high student matched ATCG to ATCG, so we are adding a DNA puzzle kit.
notes.excerpt_note: Aachen chains feedback to change step by step. Heidelberg gives one specific belief and its answer.
notes.ballot: How well did their work promote mutual learning and/or a dialogue?

notes.anchor: We employed the use of interactive feedback loops post-activity survey forms.
notes.title: This sentence is missing words
notes.body: “Interactive feedback loops post-activity survey forms” has no joining words, and the next sentence has two main verbs (“allowed” and “guided”). Read it aloud and you will hear it.
notes.after: After each activity, students filled in a feedback survey. Their answers about climate change and synthetic biology guided our next lesson.

notes.anchor: Below are five of the main points we have identified that make up parts of completely sustainable education
notes.title: Merge 7.4 into 7.5
notes.body: Section 7.4 defines five general ideas, then 7.5 repeats the same five headings with what you did. Judges want what you did. Drop 7.4 and give each heading in 7.5 one line of definition at most. Section 7.3 also repeats section 3 and could go.

notes.anchor: By making these resources available online, teachers can continue incorporating them into their own classrooms
notes.title: Show that teachers plan to reuse them
notes.body: This says teachers “can” use your materials. You already have proof that some plan to, from your own surveys. Put it here, and add download counts if your website records them.
notes.after: All three elementary teachers who answered our survey said they would keep supporting the program, and the high school homeroom teacher plans to use our lesson plans and slides. [Number] people downloaded the materials by [date].
notes.excerpt_note: Queens names the materials, who holds them, and how another team can reuse them.
notes.ballot: Is it documented in a way that others can build upon?

notes.anchor: we hope that the materials and ideas developed through ReLeaf can continue to be shared
notes.title: End on a result and a next step
notes.body: “We hope” endings carry no information, and judges see them on many pages. End with what you did and who will continue it.
notes.after: This year we taught 144 students at five schools and put our lesson plans, slides and games online for free. In [year], [who] will [next step].
notes.excerpt_note: Even winners slip here: EPFL closes on “positive response” with no number.
